headline: COVID Inquiry Findings Spark Parliamentary Clash Over Lockdowns and $60B Pandemic Spending
summary: A royal commission’s final report on New Zealand’s COVID-19 response prompted sharp disagreement over lockdown decisions, vaccine advice and pandemic spending, with the Government promising a formal response by July. MPs also debated a proposed online casino licensing regime amid concerns about gambling harm and advertising, while cost-of-living pressures and fuel security featured in heated exchanges. Three other bills completed committee consideration and are due for further House stages.

topicSummaries.topic: COVID Inquiry Report Reopens Dispute Over Lockdowns, Vaccine Advice and Spending
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The commission’s findings revisit decisions with lasting effects on families, businesses, public services, household costs and the Government’s capacity to respond to future crises.
topicSummaries.content: Health Minister Simeon Brown said the commission found New Zealand’s initial pandemic response was appropriate, but that some later restrictions went beyond public health advice and pandemic spending was not sufficiently targeted. He cited the $60 billion COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund, which covered 821 programmes, and said the Government would respond to the report’s recommendations by July. Labour leader Chris Hipkins challenged Brown’s account of whether ministers received vaccine advice and disputed claims about Auckland lockdowns, while arguing the report also praised the country’s overall response. ACT and NZ First MPs pressed the former Government over the consequences of its decisions; Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said the report underplayed iwi-led responses and the effects on Māori and Pacific communities.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The royal commission specifically found that Ministers were not presented with the advice that the Minister has just claimed they were presented with.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The reality is that that advice was provided to the Ministers, and the mandates that it related to continued to stay in effect for some time after that.

topicSummaries.topic: Online Casino Bill Advances With Up to 15 Licences Proposed
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed regime would regulate online casino operators and advertising, while shaping protections for consumers, including young people and those at risk of gambling harm.
topicSummaries.content: The committee agreed to Parts 1 to 5 of the Online Casino Gambling Bill, but reported progress rather than completing its consideration; the bill is due back in committee. The bill would allow up to 15 licences and permit both domestic and offshore operators to apply. Internal Affairs Minister Brooke van Velden said a capped, competitive market could draw consumers away from unregulated operators and that regulations would set advertising and harm-minimisation rules. Opposition and Green MPs questioned whether the regime could increase gambling, whether offshore operators could be effectively held accountable, and whether safeguards should be written more firmly into the bill. Amendments seeking fewer licences, limits on deposits and losses, stronger advertising restrictions and other protections were defeated. The minister said the proposed community return would be handled through the Budget process, with Cabinet deciding the amount, rather than a legislated 25 percent ring-fence. She outlined a planned start from 1 May, with further transition dates for operators and the gambling duty, but the bill remains under consideration.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ingrid Leary (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: I would say that the answer is that competition will increase gambling, and, therefore, I would like to understand how increasing gambling within this regulated market is going to decrease harm.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Putting 15 companies into a regulated market makes for a safer market.

topicSummaries.topic: Rent and Real Wages Put Economic Recovery Claims Under Pressure
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Rents rising faster than many households’ incomes can put pressure on budgets even as the Government points to improving economic indicators.
topicSummaries.content: Labour leader Chris Hipkins challenged Prime Minister Christopher Luxon over a reported near-10 percent annual rise in rents and questioned whether workers’ pay was keeping pace with inflation. Luxon said rents had stabilised after increasing under the previous Government and pointed to economic growth, lower inflation and rising building consents as signs of recovery. He attributed construction difficulties to earlier spending and high interest rates; Labour cited lower construction activity and company liquidations as evidence that the sector remained under strain. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said global uncertainty made inflation forecasts difficult but said the Government wanted wages to rise faster than prices.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why does he believe that rents going up 10 percent in a year is a sign that they’ve stabilised?

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I’d just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.

topicSummaries.topic: Fuel Security Debate Links Middle East Tensions to Energy Policy
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Disruptions to global oil supplies and decisions about domestic energy infrastructure can affect fuel availability, power costs and household budgets.
topicSummaries.content: Associate Energy Minister Shane Jones said New Zealand had about 25 days of diesel and 27 days of petrol, with further supplies on the way, and warned that Middle East instability could affect imports. He argued that the closure of Marsden Point increased reliance on imported fuel; Hipkins countered that the refinery had itself relied on imported crude. In a separate exchange, Luxon defended a proposed liquefied natural gas import terminal as a way to reduce dry-year electricity risks and costs, while Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said it would deepen reliance on fossil fuels. The Speaker declined Labour’s request for an urgent debate on the Government’s response to rising oil prices.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does his decision to pour $1 billion - plus of taxpayer money into a new liquefied natural gas (LNG) import terminal instead of, say, distributed renewable energy generation increase or decrease our exposure to and dependence on risky and volatile fossil fuels?

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Building this facility takes that risk premium down, and, as I’ve said before, this will save Kiwis about $265 million a year, or about $50 a household, and will actually protect 2,000 jobs from higher energy prices.

topicSummaries.topic: Public Service and Finance Reforms Advance Despite Opposition Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bills affect how public agencies plan, report performance and publish the rules that government bodies make, with implications for accountability and access to information.
topicSummaries.content: The Public Service Amendment Bill completed committee consideration without amendment and is scheduled for its third reading next sitting day. Labour and the Greens argued that changes to Public Service responsibilities and long-term insights briefings warranted more time and cross-party agreement; Minister Judith Collins said the changes clarify chief executives’ responsibilities and consolidate briefings through the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet. The Public Finance Amendment Bill was reported with amendments, including new strategic-intentions reporting, while an Opposition proposal requiring 10-year capital management plans was defeated. The Legislation Amendment Bill, which aims to make primary and secondary legislation easier to find online, was also reported with amendments. MPs raised questions about access, cybersecurity and safeguards for published rules; it too is scheduled for a third reading next sitting day.

keyExchanges.speaker: Francisco Hernandez (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: There has not been broad cross-party agreement on this.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Judith Collins (National)
keyExchanges.quote: There is no reason to delay this.

topicSummaries.topic: Healthy Futures Amendment Bill Passes Second Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would put greater emphasis on measurable health targets and performance, which could influence how services and resources are managed across the health system.
topicSummaries.content: The House agreed by 68 votes to 55 to give the Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) Amendment Bill its second reading, following approval of Health Committee amendments. National MP Carlos Cheung argued that clear targets can strengthen accountability and help direct resources, and the bill will proceed to its next stage.

conclusion: The sitting advanced several legislative changes, but the central political divide remained over whether regulation and economic recovery plans will protect the public from the costs and risks MPs say they are meant to address.
